articles.title: Miliband tells Iran minister UK will not tolerate 'hostile activity' on British soil
articles.summary: The foreign secretary stresses "the UK's unwavering resolve to combat threats from Iranian-linked groups in UK soil, including attacks on the British Jewish community".
articles.body:
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has told Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi that the UK will "not tolerate intimidation, threats or hostile activity on UK soil".

The ministers met face-to-face at the UN General Assembly in New York City.

The Foreign Office said Miliband spoke to his counterpart about "the UK's unwavering resolve to combat threats from Iranian-linked groups in UK soil, including attacks on the British Jewish community", and discussed war in the Middle East and a British couple detained in Iran.

There was no immediate comment from Araghchi. The Islamic Republic News Agency reported the men met and "discussed bilateral ties and international developments during their talks".

Miliband's comments follow an arson attack on four Jewish community ambulances in Golders Green in March and other incidents.

The BBC understands that British intelligence chiefs were initially keeping an open mind as to whether the Iranian state or organisations working for it had a role in the Hatzola ambulance attack and other attacks against Jewish communities during 2026.

They later concluded that secret intelligence pointed to Iran or its proxies being involved in the attack.

In July, a small power plant in the UK was also shut down due to a cyber attack, which the Telegraph reported was carried out by hackers affiliated to the Iranian regime.

The Foreign Office said Miliband also spoke to his counterpart about the country's war with the US, telling Araghchi that Iran should choose "de-escalation and diplomacy instead of prolonging the war" and stressing the importance of reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

In February, the US and Israel attacked Iran, killing the country's supreme leader.

Iran responded by launching strikes on Israel and neighbouring Gulf Arab states which host US military bases. It also effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, impacting the global economy.

On Wednesday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told the UN General Assembly that any deal would have to include an end to the US blockade stopping Iranian ships from using the waterway.

Responding to US President Donald Trump's threat to "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if a deal is not reached soon, Pezeshkian said his country will never "bend the knee" .

"The resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying," he said.

There was no immediate comment from the US, whose delegation walked out of the chamber at the start of Pezeshkian's address.

The Foreign Office said Miliband also used Thursday's meeting to raise the detention of British couple Lindsay and Craig Foreman in Iran.

The couple, who are from East Sussex, have been detained for more than 20 months after being arrested while passing through the country on a motorcycle journey.

In February, the Foremans were each sentenced to 10 years in jail on espionage charges, which they deny.

In Miliband's discussion with the Iranian foreign minister, he reiterated the call for them to be immediately released and stressed that their welfare remains a priority for the government, the Foreign Office said.

articles.title: Pittsburgh pediatric doctor fatally stabbed and wife wounded in attack as they slept
articles.summary: Elijah Hemingway, 32, was found behind a nearby home and arrested in connection with the stabbings of Dr. Idris Evans and his wife.
articles.body: A Pittsburgh pediatric doctor was killed and his wife was wounded when they were brutally stabbed while they slept in their bed, police said Thursday. Police responded to a home in Edgewood on Thursday shortly after midnight and found Idris Evans, 46, and his wife with “multiple stab wounds,” Allegheny County police said. Evans, a pediatric critical care physician at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center’s Children’s Hospital of Pittsburgh, was taken to a hospital, where he was pronounced dead, police said. His wife was also taken to a hospital and remains in critical condition. During a search, detectives found Elijah Hemingway, 32, behind a nearby home, with “lacerations to his hand,” police said. He was detained and taken to an area hospital for treatment. Court records show Hemingway is awaiting a preliminary hearing on charges of criminal homicide, aggravated assault, burglary, criminal trespass and possessing instruments of crime. At the hospital, Evans’ wife told authorities that she and her husband awoke to a man stabbing them with a kitchen knife. She described the man as “psychotic,” saying he repeatedly “made utterances about ‘God’ and being ‘God,’” according to the criminal complaint. She also described the man as being in his underwear. Allegheny County Assistant Police Superintendent Victor Joseph said at a news conference Thursday that police are investigating whether Evans and Hemingway might have known each other. “The wife believes she heard her husband say a name, Elijah, but the wife is also unclear if the actor identified himself by name, so we’re still investigating that,” Joseph said. Evans’ wife indicated she did not know the suspect herself, the complaint says. She said that the man also used other objects in their bedroom as weapons and that she and her husband fought back as best they could. She successfully yelled for her children, ages 8 and 12, to flee and go to their neighbor’s house, according to the complaint. The children were uninjured, police said. Evans’ wife said that the man demanded her car keys and that she gave them to him, the filing said. Evans’ wife, who was stabbed multiple times, ran to a neighbor’s house for help and to call 911, according to the complaint. When police arrived at the couple’s home, they found Evans on the floor of the third-story bedroom, with “multiple severe stab wounds and lacerations to his trunk,” the complaint says. There was a large amount of what was believed to be blood on the floor and walls of the bedroom, which was in disarray, with items knocked over. In the third-story bathroom, police found a large kitchen knife, also with suspected blood on it, the complaint says. The back door of the home was found open with blood on the handle. Officers also noticed an open kitchen window with suspected blood at its base and a “Leatherman style multi-tool nearby,” the filing says. In an interview with police, Hemingway said Evans had invited him to the residence hours before and let him inside when he arrived on his bike, the complaint says. However, no bike was found at the property, it says. Hemingway claimed that Evans attacked him with a knife and that a physical altercation ensued between himself and both victims in the third-floor bedroom, according to the complaint. Hemingway said that during the struggle, he was stabbed in the back, it says. He did not have any visible injuries beyond those to his hands, the complaint says. He remains in the hospital. It was not immediately clear whether he has an attorney. Joseph said that Hemingway does not live in the Edgewood area and that he did not immediately have information about whether Hemingway had a criminal history. The investigation continues. Evans’ death has shaken the local medical community. In addition to working as a physician, Evans was an assistant professor of critical care medicine at the University of Pittsburgh. The school and the hospital are “deeply saddened by the tragic loss of Dr. Idris Evans,” a hospital spokesperson said in a statement. “Dr. Evans was a dedicated caregiver and valued member of our hospital and university communities. Our thoughts are with his family, loved ones, and colleagues during this difficult time. We ask that their privacy be respected,” the statement said.

articles.title: “I did my office work in incognito mode, and it got me a promotion”: Man shares tips that can help in the career growth of corporate employees
articles.summary: A workplace story shared by a man named Harshit Mahawar has sparked discussion online after he claimed that regularly using incognito mode while working
articles.body: A workplace story shared by a man named Harshit Mahawar has sparked discussion online after he claimed that regularly using incognito mode while working helped create an unusual impression among his employers and colleagues. According to Mahawar, he uses private browsing for his office work because he believes employers monitor employees' browsing activity. However, his claim should be treated as a personal account rather than proof that using incognito mode can lead to faster promotions. Incognito or private browsing generally prevents the browser from saving certain information, such as local browsing history and cookies after a session. It does not make a user's online activity invisible to an employer, network administrator or internet service provider.He says private browsing became part of his work routineIn a video, Mahawar explained why he chooses to use incognito mode while working. He said, “Main apna sara office work incognito mode me karta hoon aur main koi moorkh nahi hoon kyunki humare employers humara browsing data track karte hain. Aur guess karo wo sabse kadi monitoring kiski karte honge? Private browsing.” Mahawar appears to suggest that private browsing gives him an additional layer of privacy while using his workplace computer. His comments also reflect a common misunderstanding about what incognito mode actually does. Private browsing can stop the browser from retaining certain records locally, but it is not designed to prevent employers from monitoring activity on company devices or networks. Depending on an organisation's systems and policies, employers may still have other ways of monitoring network traffic, device activity or access to workplace resources.He links incognito browsing to three unexpected benefitsMahawar went on to claim that the habit has produced three major benefits in his professional life. He said, “Is habit ke mujhe 3 behatreen results dikhe hain. 1. Doors are better, with hikes and perks. 2. 3 saal me freshers se VP banne wala main youngest employee hoon. 3. Colleagues mere success se confused hai kyunki meri browsing history me kuch hai hi nahi.” According to his account, he believes the absence of browsing history has contributed to how colleagues perceive his work habits. He also claimed that he has received better salary hikes and perks and that he became the youngest employee to rise from a fresher to a vice president in three years. There is no information in the provided account independently verifying that his use of incognito mode caused these professional outcomes. Promotions, salary increases and career progression can depend on many factors, including performance, responsibilities, skills, experience and organisational decisions.‘History is created by those who leave no browser history’Mahawar ended his video with a humorous line that appears to have become the central message of his story. He said, “Ek baat yaad rakhna doston, ‘History is created by those who leave no browser history.’” The statement plays on the word “history”, turning a technical feature of private browsing into a joke about professional success. While the claim may be entertaining, employees should not assume that using incognito mode will hide their online activity from their employer. Google's Chrome guidance, for example, notes that incognito mode limits what is saved on the device but does not necessarily prevent activity from being visible to employers, schools or other organisations that manage the network.Ultimately, Mahawar's story is best understood as an unusual workplace anecdote rather than evidence of a career strategy. His experience may have generated attention because of the contrast between an apparently empty browser history and his claimed professional rise, but there is no established psychological or workplace principle suggesting that private browsing itself leads to faster promotions.You use AI every day. articles.title: Young men flee Tigray amid fears of forced recruitment
articles.summary: Years after the war, unresolved tensions are again leaving young people fearful of being drawn into fighting.
articles.body:
Tigray, Ethiopia – Gebru, 27, says he was taken from his neighbourhood to a local administration office with other young men. His parents feared he would be sent to fight and searched for a way to get him out. They eventually paid to secure his release, he says.

“I was taken to the office with other young men. My parents found a way to get me released by paying 20,000 [Ethiopian] birr ($123) in cash.”

After he was released, Gebru left Tigray for Addis Ababa.

“My parents were afraid that if I stayed, I would be taken again. They told me to leave Tigray and save myself.”

Gebru is among young men who say they are leaving Tigray because they fear being forcibly recruited to fight as political and military tensions rise in the northern Ethiopian region.

Nearly four years after the November 2022 Pretoria Agreement ended the war between Ethiopia’s federal government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), reports of forced recruitment and military mobilisation have raised fears among young conflict survivors that they could once again be drawn into fighting.

The African Union-brokered agreement ended two years of war in Tigray, but key issues – including contested territory, the return of displaced people and the disarmament of Tigrayan forces – remain unresolved.

Human Rights Watch reported in July that Tigrayan authorities and forces had forcibly recruited civilians, including children as young as 15, since at least April. The organisation documented cases involving former combatants and other men and boys who it said were taken from streets, homes, workplaces and gold-mining areas.

The allegations come as tensions between the federal government and the TPLF have risen, with both sides accusing the other of military mobilisation. Heavy fighting was also reported near Ethiopia’s border with Sudan in August.

For some young men, the response has been to leave.

Shewit, 24, had been trying to rebuild his life after the war. He was studying at Mekelle University, running a language-class business he had started about a year earlier and helping to look after his younger siblings.

But as reports of recruitment and military mobilisation increased, he said staying in Tigray began to feel unsafe.

“I had already survived one war. I didn’t want to go through another,” he told Al Jazeera.

He eventually left for Addis Ababa, leaving behind his family, his studies and his business.

“I left behind my siblings, who depended on me, and a business I had sacrificed so much to build.”

He says he does not want to return unless he can bring his family with him.

“I don’t want to go back. In fact, if I can, I want to bring my family and my siblings here with me.”

Gebrehiwot, 28, is still in Tigray. He fought during the previous war but says he does not want to return to the battlefield.

He says the experience changed the way he viewed the war’s political and military leadership, particularly after seeing wounded fighters and families of dead soldiers struggle after the fighting ended.

“We were told that we were fighting for our people, but after the war ended, I saw wounded fighters and families of the dead being abandoned.”

He says reports that former combatants were being called back increased his fears.

“Former combatant friends were being called back to the army and I heard some had been taken away forcibly. I was afraid I would be next, so I left my hometown and moved to Mekelle, hoping I would not get identified here.”

Unlike Shewit and Gebru, he has not left Tigray. But he says his experience of the previous war makes the prospect of another mobilisation difficult to contemplate.

“I know what the battlefield looks like. I don’t want to go back there and risk not coming home.”

Human Rights Watch says the recruitment allegations extend beyond former fighters to civilians and young people.

“We found that both former fighters but also civilians – young men, sometimes boys – were being abducted, detained,” said Laetitia Bader, the organisation’s Horn of Africa director. “Sometimes in the streets, in marketplaces, also in mining areas which is an important form of livelihood in the region.”

Bader said Human Rights Watch had documented cases involving minors as young as 15.

The organisation also said a mobilisation proclamation introduced in June criminalised desertion and attempts by relatives to prevent loved ones from being conscripted.

For young people who survived the previous war, Bader said, the reported recruitment was another reason to flee.

“The forced conscription continues to have an impact. Young people continue to try to flee the region not only because of the forced conscription but also the devastating humanitarian situation in the region,” she said.

The TPLF has disputed allegations of forced recruitment, saying young people were joining voluntarily. TPLF spokesman Michael Asgedom previously described the allegations as a “mistaken narrative”.

Al Jazeera contacted Asgedom for a response to the allegations in this story, but he did not respond to calls or text messages.

Muauz Gidey Alemu, an assistant professor of political science and lead researcher at the Tigray Institute of Policy Studies, said the recruitment should be understood within a broader political and security crisis that followed the Pretoria Agreement.

“The emergence of forced conscription at this particular moment should not be understood simply as a military recruitment exercise,” he said. “It is better understood as a symptom of the deeper political and security crisis that has developed around the incomplete implementation of the Pretoria Cessation of Hostilities Agreement.”

Gidey said the agreement had stopped large-scale fighting but had not resolved all the political and security issues surrounding the post-war period.

“The present situation demonstrates that Pretoria produced an effective cessation of large-scale warfare but an incomplete peace settlement,” he said.

He said continued mobilisation could create a cycle in which insecurity fuels military recruitment, which then deepens insecurity.

“Political insecurity generates military mobilisation; military mobilisation reinforces political insecurity; political insecurity then becomes an argument for further mobilisation,” Gidey said.

For the young men interviewed by Al Jazeera, however, the question is less about the political calculations driving mobilisation than about whether they can avoid being pulled back into war.

Gebru says leaving became his way of protecting himself.

“After what happened, I knew I could not stay there and live normally. I felt that the only way to protect myself was to leave.”

Shewit is now in Addis Ababa, separated from his family and the life he had been rebuilding.

“I didn’t leave because I wanted to. I left because I wanted to have a chance to build a future.”

Gebrehiwot, who remains in Tigray, says his hopes are simpler.

“I don’t want anything extraordinary. I just want to live peacefully, stay with my family and never have to pick up a gun again.”

articles.title: Yung Filly: British rapper to face eight-day retrial in June 2027
articles.summary: Andres Felipe Valencia Barrientos was cleared of several sexual offences in July but a jury was undecided on three rape charges.
articles.body:
British rapper Yung Filly will face a rape retrial in Australia next June after a jury failed to reach a verdict during an earlier trial.

In July, a jury acquitted the 31-year-old - whose real name is Andres Felipe Valencia Barrientos - of three counts of rape, one of assault and one of strangulation but found him guilty of two assault charges. No decision was reached for three rape charges, which he has denied.

A fan, aged 20 at the time, alleges Barrientos repeatedly raped and assaulted her in his hotel room in Perth, Western Australia, after a 2024 concert.

The court previously heard that Barrientos and the woman had consensual sex before she alleged it turned violent and he refused to stop.

On Friday, Perth's District Court set 15 June as the start date for the retrial which is expected to last eight days.

Barrientos was not required to appear in court and is understood to have returned to the UK after the court granted him permission to leave Australia as part of his bail conditions.

Sentencing for the two assault charges that the jury found Barrientos guilty of in July will take place after the retrial.

Barrientos, who was born in Colombia and brought up in the UK, is known for his work with the YouTube collective Beta Squad.

He has appeared in the celebrity version of Bake Off on Channel 4 and presented BBC Three shows.

articles.title: Nepal’s leader, at U.N., says recent floods serve as a ‘warning to the world’ about climate change
articles.summary: “We did not create this crisis, yet we are paying a colossal price for it,” said Prime Minister Balendra Shah, whose nation contributes less than one-tenth of 1% of global greenhouse gases.
articles.body: UNITED NATIONS — Nepal’s prime minister scolded fellow world leaders Thursday, saying the nation’s recent deadly flood reminds a warming world that climate change keeps hurting people who didn’t cause the crisis but now need help. The August disaster “was not just a local tragedy. It was a warning to the world. And I ask you today: Have you really heard that warning?” Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah said at the U.N. General Assembly on Thursday night. “Nearly three years ago, standing in the shadow of our Mount Everest, the secretary-general of the United Nations warned humanity about the madness and impending climate disaster.” “That cry from the rooftop of the world was not heard enough,” Shah said. “We in Nepal heard it. Our communities heard it. Scientists around the world heard it. They repeated it with evidence. But we, the political leaders, have been negligent to translate those warnings in action at the speed and scale that the vulnerable people require.” International scientists have connected melting permafrost from climate change — caused by burning coal, oil and gas — to the instability of the glacier, which partly collapsed and triggered a massive flood that has killed at least 1,400 people with even more still missing. Shah said that Nepal contributed less than one-tenth of 1% of the heat-trapping gases behind climate change. About 99% of Nepal’s electricity comes from hydropower, and many workers were trapped in tunnels by the flooding. “We did not create this crisis, yet we are paying a colossal price for it,” said Shah, 36, a former rapper and engineer who is the youngest head of government to address the General Assembly this year. “Our glaciers are retreating, our mountain slopes are becoming unstable, our rivers are becoming less predictable, and every major disaster threatens to erase years of development.” In a black Dhaka topi, a traditional brimless Nepali hat, Shah spoke while wearing his signature dark sunglasses, which he uses for medical reasons. He said “the tragic consequences of a warming climate” tell the world that “climate change does not recognize borders. Glaciers and floods do not travel with stamps and passports.” Subeksha Khadka, a humanitarian and former Miss Nepal International, in an online interview, praised Shah’s speech and echoed the warning: “This time Nepal has been on the target, but it could be anyone. This is our story right now, and it can be anybody else’s tomorrow. So it’s time to act.” Shah didn’t ask for a specific amount in aid, but he called the international financial aid system inadequate and too bureaucratic. This included a loss and damage fund agreed upon a few years ago for poor nations hit by climate disasters not of their own making. “Climate finance must not become another bureaucratic maze through which vulnerable countries spend years” maneuvering when they need help. “When the house is burning, we do not ask a family to complete 50 forms. We act. This is what climate justice means.” He exhorted the General Assembly to act on relief, rehabilitation, reconstruction — which are traditional international help concepts — but also “responsibility, reparation, resilience.” Reparation is a word and an issue that rankles industrial Western nations like the United States, which is historically the world’s biggest carbon emitter. Over the past 75 years, the United States has spewed about 1,500 times more carbon into the air than Nepal has, according to the Global Carbon Project, a group of scientists who track greenhouse gas emissions by countries. Historical emissions matter because carbon dioxide stays in the atmosphere for more than a century, trapping heat. The U.S. this week announced $31 million in aid to Nepal for flood recovery, which brings America’s total financial help up to $36 million. It’s less than 1% of what they need. “Preliminary assessments indicate that from recent disaster alone, Nepal has suffered loss of over $5 billion, nearly 15% of our GDP and a third of our annual budget,” Shisir Khanal, Nepal’s foreign minister, said Wednesday at the U.N. climate summit. “Thus for Nepal, this catastrophe is not merely a humanitarian emergency. It is a development emergency dismantling years of progress. It is a justice crisis exposing the inequities of global climate action, and it is an existential crisis striking at the very survival of our communities and our future.” “What happened in Nepal is not an isolated disaster, but a preview of what awaits many vulnerable nations,” Khanal said. Former U.S. Vice President Al Gore said in an interview that Nepal’s disaster shows that the climate crisis “was getting worse much faster” than people can handle and foreshadows problems with melting glaciers that feed all of the great rivers of Asia, putting the water supply of 2 billion people at risk.

articles.title: Scam booking sent Loughborough family to Wetherspoon pub near Tower Bridge
articles.summary: Which? says staff are turning away up to 20 tourists a day after scammers used the pub's address.
articles.body:
A theatre-goer fell victim to a "sophisticated phishing attack" after booking a "luxury" London apartment, only to discover the address was a Wetherspoon pub.

Paul Dawson, from Loughborough in Leicestershire, paid £73 for a one-night stay for his family via Booking.com at The London Crown apartments to watch the musical Hamilton in the West End.

Days later, he said, he discovered the address shown in the listing was actually The Liberty Bounds pub, a Wetherspoon near Tower Bridge.

Consumer protection organisation Which? said Wetherspoon staff had been turning away up to 20 tourists a day after scammers used the pub's address as a listing for a "block of luxury apartments".

Which? said it was also made aware of a property listed as "Apartments near Big Ben", with the address given as Portcullis House, part of the House of Commons estate, where hundreds of MPs work.

Booking.com told Which? that in both cases, listings for legitimate properties had been targeted by a "sophisticated phishing attack, allowing criminals to hijack the listings".

Wetherspoon said it had informed Booking.com about this scam "as soon as it came to their attention".

Dawson, 55, made his booking in August. Two days later, he said he received an email from The London Crown containing a link to a fake Booking.com page, which asked for his bank details.

Dawson told Which? he contacted Booking.com with his suspicions, but said the platform told him that he would need to visit the "fake apartment" and wait until after 7pm before it would relocate him.

This was despite Mr Dawson explaining to them that he had since discovered the address shown in the listing was actually The Liberty Bounds pub.

He told Which?: "I explained to the support staff that I had autistic children and the idea of turning up at a clearly non-existent property at 10.30pm would have been catastrophic.

"This did not change their response, that I needed to go to the property. They said that if it was not possible to check in then I could contact them again and they would find an alternative."

Dawson said the family ended up staying in the Premier Inn in Goodge Street.

The listing for the London Crown apartments had 250 negative reviews from August and September along with a handful of, likely fake, positive reviews, Which? said.

The BBC checked the listing on Thursday. The information was still visible but the page carried the message: "We're sorry, but this property isn't taking reservations on our site right now".

Wetherspoon said the listing was removed only for it to reappear, "though it now appears that the ability to book has been blocked".

"We have again notified them [Booking.com], asking for the listing to be permanently removed.

"It is clearly unacceptable for people to be defrauded in such a flagrant manner.

"This is upsetting for the pub team, as there is little they can do to help, but even more so for the people who have been misled and have lost money as a result.

"Booking.com urgently needs to adopt more robust procedures to prevent fraudulent listings like this appearing in the first place."

Many of the reviews from customers said they told Booking.com that it was a scam but had been ignored.

One customer said: "I reported it to Booking.com three days before check-in but they refused to do anything."

Another customer, from Spain, complained that she and her friend had been left stranded, writing: "Two girls alone in London at two o'clock in the morning with no accommodation."

Booking.com also has an AI trip planner called Dot, which allows users to ask questions. On The London Crown listing page a Which? researcher asked: "Is this a real property, or is it a scam?".

It replied: "The London Crown is a legitimate property located in the centre of London. It offers various amenities such as free wifi, free bikes, and free private parking. It is conveniently located near Longleat Safari Park and Longleat House, with London City Airport just 10km away. Based on the detailed description and amenities listed, the London Crown appears to be a real and well-equipped property."

Dot failed to recognise that Longleat Safari Park was more than 100 miles (160km) from London, in Wiltshire.

"Apartments near Big Ben" and The London Crown apartments were both targeted by the phishing attack, said Booking.com.

"The attack affected the properties' own computer systems and gave cybercriminals temporary, unauthorised access to the accommodation's Booking.com account," a spokesperson said.

"We take incidents like this extremely seriously, and suspended bookings at both properties, as well as supporting affected customers."

An Ofcom spokesperson said: "Fraud online can have serious consequences for victims and platforms have clear legal duties to take down illegal content generated by users once they become aware of it.

"More broadly, we've shown that we'll use our enforcement powers against platforms that fail to comply with the Online Safety Act, and have already launched investigations into over 100 sites."

articles.title: Tata v Tata: What’s behind India’s big boardroom brawl?
articles.summary: India’s most famous conglomerate is knee-deep in feuds over who gets to decide the Tata Group’s future.
articles.body:
New Delhi, India – An unprecedented power struggle has erupted at the top of one of India’s largest conglomerates, pitting the board of its holding company Tata Sons against its majority shareholder Tata Trusts.

Last week, Tata Sons extended Chairman N Chandrasekaran’s term and said it would consider publicly listing the holding company, flying in the face of the family charity that controls the 158-year-old Tata Group.

Extending Chandrasekaran’s chairmanship and taking Tata public is at the heart of the family-linked feud – and its outcome will not be limited merely to the group’s headquarters at Bombay House.

Collectively, listed Tata companies have a market capitalisation of $277bn and influence over 17.7 million retail shareholders apart from pension funds, insurers and mutual funds, investment advisory firm InGovern said.

So what’s behind the bitter brawl inside one of the corporate world’s most consequential boardrooms?

The Tata Group business conglomerate spans industries from information technology and automobiles to steel, power, aviation, chemicals and consumer goods.

It has 26 publicly listed companies, including TCS and Tata Motors. They have a combined market capitalisation of $277bn and operate across more than 100 countries. Tata Sons serves as the group’s principal holding and investment company.

The group’s humble beginnings go back more than 150 years when Nusserwanji Tata, born into a Parsi priest’s family in Gujarat, moved to Mumbai (then Bombay) in the mid-19th century and entered the trading business.

He later expanded into trade with China before his son Jamsetji Tata built the business into an industrial group, riding on deals in cotton and opium. Opium was then banned by China’s Qing rulers, and Nusserwanji found a way to smuggle it.

The conglomerate’s real breakthrough came when the United States Civil War broke out in 1861. The disruption to US cotton supplies sent Indian cotton prices soaring and transformed the fortunes of Bombay’s merchants, including the Tatas.

Their businesses turned into an empire over coming generations. Jamsetji Tata died in 1904, and his sons Dorabji and Ratanji Tata carried his businesses forward. The family’s charitable trusts became major shareholders of Tata Sons.

JRD Tata, who became chairman in 1938, transformed the group into a diversified industrial enterprise, expanding into aviation, including India’s flagship carrier, Air India; chemicals; and engineering. In 1991, Ratan Tata succeeded JRD, taking over as India began economic liberalisation.

Under Ratan, the Tata Group consolidated a sprawling group under a more unified corporate identity and pushed it onto the global stage with landmark acquisitions, including Tetley, Corus and Jaguar Land Rover. Tata is now pushing into the next generation of global manufacturing with a major iPhone assembly operation in India and a semiconductor fabrication and chip-assembly business.

Ratan was the chairman of both Tata Sons and its majority stakeholder, Tata Trusts, and remained a bridge between the two. After he died in 2024, a widening schism gradually became apparent.

Tata Trusts is an umbrella of family-linked charities that own 66 percent of Tata Sons.

The face-off was triggered on September 17 when Tata Sons reappointed Chandrasekaran as its chairman over the Tata Trusts’ nominee on the board, Noel Tata, in a 4-to-1 vote.

Noel Tata is the sitting chairman of Tata Trusts and the only family-linked senior executive sitting in the top echelons of Tata Sons today. Noel is the half-brother of Ratan Tata and became Tata Trusts’ chairman after Ratan’s death in 2024.

But the divisions between the company and majority shareholder run deeper – and include questions of taking Tata Sons public and providing a planned exit to Tata Sons’ second-largest shareholder, Shapoorji Pallonji.

Last month, Chandrasekaran said he would not seek another term as chairman after February 2027. But Tata Group said in a statement the board asked him to reconsider the group’s “larger interests”, a request that he accepted.

The 68-year-old Noel Tata called the reappointment “illegal” under Tata Sons’ articles of association, adding in a statement that both trust nominees on the board were required to vote in coordination, whereas only Noel Tata voted against. The other trust nominee, Venu Srinivasan, voted in favour of Chandrasekaran’s reappointment.

This matter is now expected to be decided by the courts.

India’s central bank, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), requires companies with assets exceeding $10.45bn to publicly list.

Tata Sons tried to skirt the requirements by deregistering as a nonbank finance company. But days before its board meeting this month, the RBI rejected the company’s request, bringing it closer to a public listing.

Tata’s structure is unusual because the holding company at the very top of the empire is at the moment not itself subject to public-market scrutiny, even though many of the companies beneath it are.

At the board meeting, Tata Sons said it would take steps to comply with the RBI’s requirements. But Noel Tata opposed the move, arguing that listing would alter the character of a group that also supports extensive philanthropic ⁠activities.

The Shapoorji Pallonji Group holds ⁠an 18.4 percent stake in Tata Sons and is its second-largest shareholder.

The infrastructure and construction conglomerate is knee-deep in debt and is seeking ⁠to monetise its shareholding in Tata Sons.

Tata Trusts said Noel Tata tabled a plan to sell ‌a part of the Shapoorji Pallonji Group’s stake in the holding company worth $2.61bn. Tata Sons has not yet commented on the plan.

Shapoor Mistry, the group’s patriarch, is also Noel Tata’s brother-in-law. The Shapoorji Pallonji Group backs Tata Sons going public and is opposed to Noel’s position.

What does the dispute mean for India’s economy?

The central question in the showdown that is captivating millions of Indians involves the public listing of Tata Sons.

Noel Tata said in a statement that the Tata Group “was conceived as a national service carried on through business”. The unusual privately owned structure of Tata Sons, Noel argued, has allowed the company to remain in the country’s service and “act repeatedly in ways that a purely commercial calculus would not have supported”.

“A listing will destroy its character and strike at the heart of this principle,” Tata Trusts has argued.

However, Santosh Mehrotra, an Indian development economist, told Al Jazeera that Tata Sons needs to be listed publicly, no matter what. “There is a law for everyone, and Tata cannot be an exception to that,” he said.

“We are at a stage as a country when top business houses cannot be allowed to continue to behave in whatever manner they have managed to behave in over the last 100 years,” Mehrotra said.

Mehrotra argued that over the past decade under Prime Minister Narendra Modi, India’s top business houses, including the empires of billionaires Gauran Adani and Mukesh Ambani, “have been permitted by the government to grow the concentration of industries across sectors in a historically unprecedented manner”.

“India’s biggest business houses have grown horizontally, capturing all sectors, which have come at the cost of people below them in the pyramid,” Mehrotra said.

“That means that the core inflation is being driven essentially by these handful of businesses because their horizontal and vertical control gives them the ability to mock up prices that are unprecedented in our economy’s history while their profits mount,” he said.

Mehrotra said that while the Tata boardroom drama could be captivating for some, “ordinary Indians’ concerns are rooted in regulating the unchecked growth [of conglomerates] backed by the government.”

InGovern, a governance advisory firm, said in a note that a holding company like Tata Sons that exercises “influence over businesses of such scale cannot reasonably remain outside the governance and transparency expectations increasingly associated with systemically important financial and industrial conglomerates”.

That is slated to be decided in the courtroom now.

Both sides have lawyered up with some of India’s top legal eagles. Harish Salve, a former solicitor general of India, is leading the Tata Sons legal team while Abhishek Singhvi, a member of parliament from the opposition Indian National Congress party, is representing Tata Trusts.

The Tata Group is no stranger to boardroom tussles and dramas. After Ratan Tata stepped down from the Tata Sons chairmanship in December 2012, Cyrus Mistry was appointed to the top job, becoming the first person from outside the Tata family to lead Tata Sons in decades.

However, differences grew between Mistry and Ratan Tata, who was then still heading Tata Trusts, over strategy, governance and capital allocation. Tata Sons pulled off a stunning coup, removing Mistry as the chairman in October 2016.

Cyrus is the younger brother of Shapoor Mistry and also the brother-in-law of Noel Tata. In bitterly fought legal battles, Cyrus eventually lost his case in 2021 before the Supreme Court. At that time, lawyers Salve and Singhvi found themselves on the same side, fighting for Tata Sons against Mistry.

That judgement upheld “that the affirmative voting rights given to Tata Trusts-nominated directors are legal, valid and a globally accepted corporate norm for majority-trust-held institutions”, said Nitin Potdar, a senior company lawyer based in Mumbai.

Currently, the Tata Sons board has two nominated members from Tata Trusts: Noel Tata and Venu Srinivasan. While Noel Tata opposed the reinstatement of Chandrasekaran as the chairman of the holding company, Srinivasan voted in favour.

“Even if the two Tata Trusts nominees give their votes differently, that does not give rise to any [legal] deadlock,” Potdar told Al Jazeera.

Singhvi, who will now represent Noel Tata, wrote in an X post that his reaction to the tussle “is one of sadness and regret that these issues could not be solved amicably”.

“But in the ultimate analysis, fundamental rights of shareholder-owners cannot be nullified in the manner in which they have been,” he wrote. “To stultify shareholder ownership rights would spell doomsday for corporate governance across hundreds of Indian companies.”

“Rupturing the over hundred years of Tata Trust and Tata Sons established hyphenated relationship and divorcing one from the other seems unthinkable,” Singhvi said.

articles.body: At an age when most children are playing around in playgrounds and still mastering their first interests, a nine-year-old Indian-origin prodigy is aiming for a world record. Adrian Abraham is preparing to walk into a Grade 8 electric guitar exam and, if he passes, then into record books.The UK-based tween is a rock and metal guitarist, singer and songwriter, currently training for the exam, the highest grade in the graded music system. Passing it at nine, would make him the youngest person ever to achieve the milestone on the electric guitar, an achievement that would also earn him an official Guinness World Record.A talented artist, Abraham's technical prowess has earned him global artist sponsorships from two renowned names in rock music: Marshall Amplifiers and Solar Guitars. "I just love playing the guitar and expressing myself through rock and metal music. Preparing for my Grade 8 exam is a lot of hard work, but the thought of setting a Guinness World Record keeps me practising every day!" he told Wion.From Western metal to Indian rock tracks, the nine-year-old has a wide musical repertoire. "I also really love exploring my roots by covering great Indian tracks like the music from Rockstar," he said. "It's so cool to see people from all over the world enjoying how I mix Western rock with Bollywood elements."He also has a social media profile with a following of 5K on Instagram, where he posts renditions and covers inspired by Indian and international artists. Supporters have followed his progress online, and Abraham has earned praise from fans and artists alike.A Grade 8 exam is a challenging benchmark. It typically requires an advanced command of musical interpretation, technique, sight-reading and aural skills. articles.title: Other Voices: Festival's return to Londonderry 'a dream come true'
articles.summary: Other Voices, which is marking its 25th anniversary this year, is a two-day celebration of music, art and culture.
articles.body:
The founder and director of an internationally-acclaimed music festival has said its return to Londonderry is "a dream come true" and will help make the city "visible and audible" on the global music stage.

Other Voices, which is marking its 25th anniversary this year, is a two-day celebration of music, art and culture, with performances streamed globally online.

About 24,000 people are expected to attend events in person, generating an estimated £1.5m for the local economy.

This year's Other Voices line-up includes a mix of established artists and also emerging talent, with a strong focus on musicians from the north west. BRIT Award-winner Kate Nash is among the headline acts.

Other Voices founder Philip King said it is a "pure delight" to be coming back to Londonderry after more than a decade away.

"When we went to Derry 13 years ago as part of the UK City of Culture programme, it was a revelatory experience," he told BBC Radio Foyle's North West Today.

"There was something magical about taking the Other Voices circus to Derry and getting such a welcome, such warmth, such hospitality and such fantastic music in the city and to come back is really a dream come true."

Londonderry was chosen as the UK's inaugural City of Culture back in 2013 and went on to host more than 140 events, including the prestigious Turner Prize and the Royal Ballet's first visit to Northern Ireland in 20 years.

King said this weekend's events mark the beginning of a three-year stint for Other Voices in Derry.

"We believe that if we can build on the legacy of 13 years ago, we can turn that into something really positive.

"Coming back to Derry, I guess it will make Derry audible and visible on a world stage, and we're thrilled to be able to do that."

Siânna Ní Laithbheartaigh is from the band Tramp, who have previously played at two Other Voices events in Cardigan, Wales, and Dingle, County Kerry.

Formed in 2020, the four-piece, whose members come from Donegal, Tyrone and Derry, describe their music as a mix of indie, rock, punk and folk.

They will perform at Derry's Playhouse on Saturday as part of Other Voices, as well as many others.

Siânna said it is significant for the band to perform on a platform with global reach.

"It can feel like there aren't many opportunities in Derry to perform as a band beyond an open mic night or a bar," the lead singer said.

"It is so valuable when you have something that has a reach beyond the island of Ireland.

"Promoting yourself as a band can be really difficult, so it's extremely helpful to have an established festival like Other Voices back you."

Performances will take place across two days in some of Derry's most popular spaces and venues, including St Columb's Hall, New Gate Arts and Culture Centre, Cultúrlann Uí Chanáin, the Nerve Centre and the Playhouse.

Donegal blues musician and singer-songwriter Muireann Bradley will perform, alongside Brògeal, Derry band The Marra, UK soul artist Debbie and Dublin group Basht will also take to the stage.

Dublin four-piece Bleech 9:3, whose music has been described as '90s-infused heavy alt-grunge, will also perform at the Nerve Centre, alongside Manchester-based quartet Westside Cowboy.

The wider Music Trail will feature almost 50 live performances across the city.

The St Columb's Hall performances will be streamed globally on the Other Voices YouTube channel, with the performances also filmed for television.

King believes there may have been missed opportunities following Derry's 2013 UK City of Culture year, particularly in terms of its legacy, but is hopeful for the future.

"I think there was a palpable sense of excitement that this was the beginning of something and, unfortunately, for whatever reason, that promise or that legacy did not materialise in as enriching a way as it could have.

"I felt in 2013 and 2014 there was something in the offing, and it wasn't realised. But I think there is also something in the offing now."

articles.title: Whitestone solar farm plans prompt thousands of responses
articles.summary: MPs and councillors among those objecting to solar farm spanning Rotherham and Doncaster.
articles.body:
More than 2,750 people have responded to a consultation about plans to build what would be Europe's biggest solar farm in South Yorkshire.

The responses have been sent to the government's Planning Inspectorate as part of a complex process examining the proposals, which span areas of Doncaster and Rotherham.

The comments are not broken down into for or against, but a number of parish councils, community groups, MPs and Rotherham and Doncaster councils have objected.

The solar farm and battery storage was originally projected to cover 3,500 acres (5.5sq miles) but applicants Whitestone Net Zero said it had made "significant changes to the project design" following two rounds of consultation.

If constructed as proposed, the 750MW solar farm would extend from Conisbrough through Ravenfield, Bramley, Wickersley, Hellaby, Thurcroft, Brampton-en-le-Morthen, Anston, Aston, Whiston and towards Brinsworth.

The government wants at least 95% of Great Britain's electricity to come from "clean" sources, including renewables – such as solar and wind – and nuclear energy by 2030.

Last year, solar energy provided more than 6% of Great Britain's electricity – rising to more than 40% for a small number of half-hour periods in July.

The government is targeting 45-47 gigawatts (GW) of solar power capacity by 2030, to help meet its clean power goal, potentially rising to 54-57GW with extra rooftop solar.

That would be up from 21GW as of autumn 2025, according to government figures, although the solar industry puts current capacity at 24GW.

Whitestone Warriors, which represents residents and businesses, said it had "significant concerns" about the scale, location and cumulative impact of the development.

It said: "Our primary concern is that the project should be examined as a single integrated development, battery energy storage facilities, substations, cable routes and associated infrastructure. The cumulative impact must be assessed as a whole rather than in isolation."

"Residents are concerned that extensive solar infrastructure would fundamentally alter the character of these areas and lead to the industrialisation of significant areas of countryside and agricultural land," it added.

South Yorkshire Mayor Oliver Coppard has also objected, saying he is "well aware of the strength of feeling in communities".

"If successful, this scheme will be one of the largest solar farms in the UK and its impact will be felt by significant swathes of South Yorkshire for a significant period of time.

"The proposed £18m community fund over 60 years seems wholly inadequate mitigation for the negative impacts, offering little incentive or financial benefit for local communities set to lose significant local amenities and access to nature."

Whitestone said new energy projects can only connect to the National Grid at locations where there is available capacity, such as Brinsworth. Once it had secured the grid connection agreement, it looked for land nearby that would be suitable for solar.

It said: "We presented our initial proposals in autumn 2024 during the first consultation. This original masterplan presented all of the land that we were considering to include in the project.

"In response to feedback from that consultation, we reduced these areas by a quarter to create offsets around homes, villages and public rights of way.

"After the second consultation in autumn 2025, we responded to feedback and further reduced these areas around homes, villages, and environmentally sensitive locations."

The application needs to go through a lengthy planning process as it is classed as a national infrastructure project. Planning inspectors can take up to six months to examine the responses before sending their recommendation to the secretary of state for a final decision.

articles.title: Betty the 'cold-stunned' turtle set for Azores release
articles.summary: Betty was washed ashore at Dunwich during storms and has been nursed back to health in Hunstanton.
articles.body:
A rare loggerhead turtle found "cold-stunned" after coastal storms is preparing to return to the sea after seven months of recovery and rehabilitation.

Named Betty by her carers, the turtle was mistaken for "debris" on Dunwich beach in Suffolk by a member of the public in February who called the British Divers Marine Life Rescue (BDMLR).

She was transferred to Hunstanton Sea Life Centre in Norfolk, where a second loggerhead turtle, called Olive, has been under care since December. Both will travel to the Azores later this month for release.

Katie Robertson, display supervisor at the centre, said: "The moment they finally get released is going to be an emotional time for us."

Both turtles were found cold-stunned - when temperatures rapidly decline and the struggle to find warmer waters can make them lethargic and experience decreased circulation.

Robertson added: "With temperatures changing in the waters during the summertime, our temperatures in the sea are increasing and it's getting into the low 20 [degrees] - which is causing them to travel further north than where they would normally travel.

"When our temperatures drop drastically compared to the Mediterranean they get cold-stunned, which basically means the surrounding water for them gets too cold."

Loggerhead turtles are the most common turtle in the Mediterranean and typically nest on beaches from Greece and Turkey to Israel and Libya.

They weigh up to 400lb (181kg) and can be up to 48 inches (1.2m) in length. The species is named for their large heads that support their powerful jaw muscles, needed for catching prey.

Since the turtles have been in the centre's care they have undergone a range of tests, including x-rays and CT scans checking for pneumonia.

Betty, who came straight to the team from the beach, underwent more specialist care.

Robertson said it was "a step-by-step process" to get Betty ready to return to the water, as they had to work to increase her body temperature very gradually every day.

Robertson said visitors had loved seeing the rescued turtles improve and that the two animals had come a long way.

She said: "When we got the all clear for both turtles, the whole team, we just had a moment where we were just so proud of all the work we've put into it but also proud of the turtles themselves."

The creatures will leave Hunstanton on Monday before travelling to The Azores in Portugal where they will be monitored for up to two weeks before they are released back into the sea.

articles.title: “My parents are more….”: Woman quits high paying corporate job after 6 years in Canada, returns to India for ageing parents and  health
articles.summary: After spending six years in Canada and building a career at Deloitte, Preeti Bisnik has decided to leave her job and return to India.
articles.body: After spending six years in Canada and building a career at Deloitte, Preeti Bisnik has decided to leave her job and return to India. Her decision is not driven by a lack of opportunities or a job loss. Instead, she says she wants to spend more time with her ageing parents, improve her own health and take a break from her corporate career. In an Instagram video posted on September 22, Preeti explained that she had resigned from her job and was preparing to return to India. She also clarified that she was not laid off and that her manager had offered her the option of taking some time off before potentially returning to the company. For Preeti, however, the decision was about priorities rather than employment. As a Canadian citizen, she can continue living and working in Canada, but she said she no longer wanted to put off spending time with her parents.Her ageing parents became the biggest reason to returnPreeti said her parents are getting older, and her mother's health has made her think more seriously about being physically present for them. She explained that her mother is dealing with glaucoma as well as difficulties with mobility and that she did not want to remain thousands of kilometres away and later regret not spending enough time with her parents. She also wants to use the knowledge she gained while studying nutrition in Canada to support her parents' health. Her plans include helping them focus on nutrition, fitness and strength. Rather than immediately looking for another job after returning, Preeti said she wants to take some time for herself and her family. She may decide next year what she wants to do professionally.Her decision also comes after a personal health and fitness journey. Preeti said she weighed around 78 kg when she moved from India to Canada. Over the next six years, her weight increased to nearly 100 kg. She has since lost around 10 kg and now wants to devote more time to improving her fitness. After years of working in a sedentary, computer-based corporate role, she said she wants to step away from that routine for a while.Why she chose to return instead of bringing her parents to CanadaPreeti's decision prompted several questions from people online, including why she could not bring her parents to Canada. She explained that moving them would not necessarily be easy, particularly because of her mother's health. According to Preeti, her mother has glaucoma and may find the long flight difficult because of her mobility issues. Her father is also elderly. She also clarified that she is not her parents' only child. She said her brothers live in the US and London, but she still wants to be physically closer to her parents during this stage of their lives. For Preeti, the decision appears to be less about choosing one country over another and more about deciding what matters most to her at this point in life.Social media users support her decisionHer announcement received a largely supportive response online. Several users praised her for prioritising her parents over a high-paying corporate career. One user wrote, "Parents are more important than any country or a job." Another commented, "If your reason is your parents, you are already blessed, and you will find work 200% there too. As blessings work always better than any luck ... all the best." A third person wrote, "Love it! All the best and wishing you and your parents well!!! It takes a lot of willpower to make such a decision. Hope the transition is stress-free and everything you hoped for!!"For now, Preeti appears ready to embrace a slower chapter, one centred on family, health and personal priorities. Her story also highlights a decision many immigrants eventually face: whether professional opportunities abroad are worth being far from ageing parents at home.You use AI every day. articles.title: Hurricane Polo lashes Mexico as Nolo strengthens near Hawaii
articles.summary: Mexico’s southwestern communities brace for Hurricane Polo, while Hawaii faces its third hurricane threat of the year.
articles.body:
Two powerful storms have gained steam and are battering opposite sides of the Pacific this week, with Hurricane Polo lashing Mexico’s southwestern coast and Nolo strengthening into a hurricane as it bears down on Hawaii.

Nolo became a hurricane on Thursday night, according to the US National Hurricane Center (NHC). The hurricane is expected to strengthen further as it turns towards Hawaii’s Big Island.

Forecasters warned the island could see 15 to 30 inches (38 to 76cm) of rain, with higher totals possible through Saturday, while the nearby island of Maui could also face life-threatening flooding.

The heaviest rain is expected to fall over the same southeastern part of the Big Island that was hit by Hurricane Lala in August, where the ground remains saturated from that earlier storm.

“There are several communities that were isolated, flooded, roads that were washed out,” said John Bravender, a warning coordination meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Honolulu. “It’s that same area that is most under threat.”

Hawaii has already been battered this year by major flooding in spring, an earthquake and two other hurricanes since mid-August. “In my 20 years of experience here, I’ve never seen three hurricane watches for the islands in the same year,” Bravender said.

Hawaii’s governor has issued an emergency proclamation, activating more than 230 members of the state’s National Guard, and schools have been closed for the rest of the week.

Hawaiian Electric, the state’s main power utility, said crews that had been restoring electricity on the island of Kauai after Hurricane Lowell earlier this month would move to Oahu, Maui and the Big Island to prepare for Nolo.

Meanwhile, Hurricane Polo has fluctuated between Category 4 and 5, the two most powerful levels on the Saffir-Simpson scale used to measure hurricane strength, as it moves along Mexico’s coast . The NHC said Polo was expected to regain Category 5 status on Friday.

In the port city of Lazaro Cardenas, in the southwestern state of Michoacan, seawater swept through homes on Thursday, leaving wooden planks and furniture scattered across the streets.

Restaurant owner Alicia Contreras said 15-foot (4.5-metre) waves had severely damaged her property. “This is huge because we have no other source of income. Now we’re just surviving,” she said.

Mexican authorities have deployed 15,000 security personnel along the coast, suspended schools and opened shelters, evacuating people from high-risk areas, though officials have not said how many.

Polo poses the greatest threat to Guerrero and Michoacan, two neighbouring states with long coastlines dotted with small ports, tourist towns and fishing villages, many of them poor communities that residents say are often left to fend for themselves during natural disasters.

Two other storms remain far from land: Hurricane Odalys in the Pacific and Tropical Storm Fay in the North Atlantic. Forecasters said a third storm, Tropical Storm Gonzalo, could pass near or over Cape Verde, an island nation off West Africa, on Friday.

The string of storms comes amid El Nino, a recurring climate pattern that warms parts of the Pacific Ocean and tends to fuel more tropical cyclone activity, while dampening the Atlantic hurricane season.

articles.title: Nationwide protests from October 2 if Gyanesh doesn't resign by Saturday: CJP's Dipke amid SIR row
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke on Friday said that the party would launch nationwide protests from October 2 if Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh
articles.body: NEW DELHI: CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke on Friday said that the party would launch nationwide protests from October 2 if Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar does not resign by Saturday.In a post on X, Dipke said CJP would begin its protest from Mumbai on Gandhi Jayanti and subsequently take the agitation to cities across India."If Gyanesh Kumar does not resign by tomorrow, CJP will begin its nationwide protest from Mumbai on 2 October, and take it to cities across India. This Gandhi Jayanti let’s pledge to save democracy," Dipke wrote.The announcement came a day after Dipke demanded Kumar's resignation and threatened to launch a "Jantar Mantar 2.0" agitation if his demand was not met.Dipke also criticised opposition parties for continuing to contest elections while alleging that the electoral process was being rigged. He argued that participating in such elections legitimises them and creates an "illusion" that they are free and fair."Yes, elections are being rigged. But when you continue to participate in rigged elections, you legitimise these elections and help maintain the illusion that they are free and fair," he said.He questioned whether opposition parties were contesting elections because they feared political extinction if they stayed away.Dipke further accused opposition parties of raising allegations of electoral manipulation selectively, depending on the state or political party involved.The CJP founder's remarks came amid a row over the functioning of the Election Commission. The Indian Express had reported that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had objected at least 14 times over the past 10 months to decisions and orders concerning voter additions, deletions, restoration and changes to the voter registration process.EC has maintained that decisions, including those related to SIR, had been unanimous and approved by both election commissioners and the chief election commissioner.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Must maintain the trust of people': Chirag Paswan urges EC to 'firmly present its side' amid SIR row
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Union minister Chirag Paswan on Friday urged the Election Commissioner to \"firmly present its side\" amid the ongoing row over the internal
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Union minister Chirag Paswan on Friday urged the Election Commissioner to "firmly present its side" amid the ongoing row over the internal disagreements in the poll panel.Speaking to reporters, Chirag said the Election Commission must retain people's trust and address their doubts about the electoral process."If such questions are being raised against the Election Commission, I believe it is also the responsibility of the Election Commission, especially the CEC, to firmly present its side," the Union minister said."I don't care what the opposition says because it is their job is to do politics. The Election Commission must maintain the trust of the people because if doubts arise in the public's mind about the electoral process itself, that would be wrong. In such a situation, the Election Commission should firmly put forth its points so that no doubts arise in the people's minds," he added.This comes after the opposition demanded Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation after an Indian Express report highlighted differences among members of the EC over the SIR of electoral rolls. The report said Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi raised formal objections on at least 14 occasions over a 10-month period against decisions and orders related to electoral-roll processes.Earlier on Thursday, leader of opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi accused the CEC of "vote chori, kanun chori, sanstha chori (vote theft, law theft, institutional theft)", calling it an "act against the nation"."The Election Commission is the institutional protector of the vote... I have shown it with proof, and there is already more than enough information to make this a 100% certainty that Indian elections, Lok Sabha elections, 2024 election, Vidhan Sabha elections are all being rigged," he said, addressing a press conference.The Election Commission, however, described the queries and observations raised by its members as part of its routine internal process. It said written notes, technical inputs and internal scrutiny were standard mechanisms to check legal compliance and protect voters' rights.The ECI further said all decisions taken by the Commission, including those related to SIR, had full legal backing and stressed that its final decisions were unanimous.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Indigenous satellite guided weapon to give air force long range strike capability
articles.summary: The Indian Air Force is set to get a new set of indigenously developed smart weapons that will improve its stand-off strike capability, with the upcoming
articles.body: The Indian Air Force is set to get a new set of indigenously developed smart weapons that will improve its stand-off strike capability, with the upcoming induction of the satellite guided variant of the Smart Anti-Airfield Weapon (SAAW). This weapon, when deployed from an optimal altitude and speed, has an advertised range of 100 km. This will give the aircraft the ability to deploy the weapon from well outside the range of most air defence weapons.The SAAW, as the name suggests has been designed to specifically target hardened ground targets such as runways, bunkers, hardened aircraft shelters and reinforced structures. The weapon has been tested from Jaguar and Su-30MKI, but is yet to be deployed from the Tejas, as per publicly available information.The Ministry of Defence has signed a Rs 810.79 crore contract with Bharat Dynamics Limited for 160 Satellite Smart Anti-Airfield Weapons, or SAT-SAAW, along with associated equipment for the Indian Air Force. The deal falls under the Buy Indian- Indian - Indigenously Designed, Developed and Manufactured (IDDM) category, reinforcing the government's push for indigenous defence manufacturing. It is reported that the price per unit is expected to go down with future batches, as the sunken costs go down.The SAT-SAAW is an air-to-ground precision-guided glide bomb that was developed indigenously by the DRDO, the weapon will carry 60% indigenous content.Unlike unguided bombs, glide bombs use deployable wings and satellite-inertial guidance to extend their range after release, allowing the launching aircraft to stay well clear of enemy air defences while still delivering a heavy payload accurately. This stand-off capability has become central to modern air campaigns.India's broader glide-bomb programme extends beyond the SAT-SAAW. The DRDO is working on fitting a small turbine engine to the existing Smart Anti-Airfield Weapon, which already has a 100-km range, a modification expected to roughly double that distance. The Gaurav class of glide bombs, in 500-kg and 1,000-kg variants, offers a similar 100-km range, while the Tactical Advanced Range Augmentation (TARA) kit converts conventional bombs into 30-km precision weapons at low cost. Private industry has also entered the space, with JSR Dynamics developing the Khagantak, a glide bomb with a claimed range of up to 120 km that has already been tested by the IAF.Globally, the trend is witnessing greater acceptability. Russia has used converted Soviet-era bombs fitted with its UMPK glide kits extensively against Ukraine, alongside the newer purpose-built UMPB, which approaches a 90-km range. The US Navy, meanwhile, has unveiled a Range Extension Kit for the Mark-80 series bomb that reportedly pushes range out to 370 km, using a small turbine engine — a figure that exceeds even the original Brahmos missile's range.Military analysts note that such weapons, first used in the Second World War as Germany's Fritz-X and Henschel Hs-293, are now re-emerging as a cost-effective alternative to expensive cruise missiles, forcing air defence networks to rely on layered countermeasures including electronic warfare and low-cost interceptors.

articles.title: Aliko Dangote, Ethiopia and Djibouti to build $600m fuel pipeline
articles.summary: The pipeline would strengthen energy security in landlocked Ethiopia, while creating jobs at Djibouti's port.
articles.body:
Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote, Ethiopia and Djibouti have agreed to develop a $660m (£500m) petroleum pipeline and storage project linking the two countries.

The project will include a 120km- (75 mile-) pipeline connecting Djibouti's Damerjog port to a distribution facility in Dewele, Ethiopia, as well as storage capacity of about 400 million litres.

It is expected to begin operations within 18 months.

Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed said the pipeline would reduce the time needed to transport fuel from Djibouti's port to the Ethiopian capital, Addis Ababa, from five days to one.

The first phase will transport key petroleum products, including jet fuel, diesel and petrol.

Speaking at the groundbreaking ceremony, Dangote said the project would strengthen Ethiopia's energy security and make its fuel supply chain more resilient.

Landlocked Ethiopia relies heavily on Djibouti's port for imports, including petroleum products. The new infrastructure is expected to reduce pressure on existing transport systems supporting industries, including transport, aviation, agriculture and construction.

Djibouti is also expected to benefit from increased port activity, job creation and higher government revenues.

The project is part of Dangote's wider expansion of infrastructure and manufacturing businesses across Africa.

Dangote Cement has production capacity of about 55 million tonnes a year, while his oil refinery in Nigeria currently has capacity to process 700,000 barrels of crude a day and is seeking to double that to 1.4 million barrels a day.

The refinery recently listed 4.1 billion ordinary shares on the Nigerian stock exchange, aiming to raise about $1.63bn (£1.2bn).

In Kenya, the company is due to break ground next week on a proposed 700,000-barrel-a-day crude oil refinery in Lamu.

articles.title: Nepal’s leader labels devastating flood a ‘warning to the world’
articles.summary: Prime Minister Balendra Shah says world leaders must act on climate change.
articles.body:
Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah has appealed for action to combat the rising threat of climate change, calling the flood that devastated his country last month “a warning to the world”.

Shah made the comments during his address to the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Thursday night. He told the gathering that the August disaster “was not just a local tragedy”, asking them the question, “Have you really heard that warning?”

Political leaders “have been negligent to translate those warnings in action at the speed and scale that the vulnerable people require,” he said.

At least 1,453 people died when a torrent of mud, rock and water struck northern Nepal and the China-Tibet border on August 26, triggered by a glacial collapse.

According to Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, 5,500 people were still missing and 13,795 had been rescued.

Researchers from the World Weather Attribution (WWA) group said in a report released last week that the disaster was not caused by a single extreme weather event, but rather a “compound crisis” shaped by long-term warming, glacier retreat, permafrost thaw and geological instability.

Shah said climate change was hurting people not responsible for the crisis but who “are paying a colossal price for it”.

He said Nepal contributed less than one-tenth of 1 percent of the heat-trapping gases behind climate change. About 99 percent of the country’s electricity comes from hydropower, and many workers were trapped in tunnels by the flooding.

“Our glaciers are retreating, our mountain slopes are becoming unstable, our rivers are becoming less predictable, and every major disaster threatens to erase years of development,” Shah said.

Shah urged the international community to help bear the cost of helping Nepal adapt to climate change.

He proposed to create a ‘Himalaya Climate Resilience Mechanism’ which would include Nepal and neighbours India and China, and would allow them to share satellite data and expertise, monitor glacial lakes and strengthen joint early warning systems.

Nepal has asked the UN’s loss and damage fund for $20m in aid, the maximum allowed, but a tiny fraction of what it needs. A preliminary assessment by the government has placed the cost of the disaster at $5bn.

The fund, established in 2022 in the aftermath of catastrophic floods in Pakistan, has yet to make even its first disbursement, and observers see Nepal as a key test of its credibility.

Earlier this week, the United States pledged an additional $31m in new flood recovery support.

articles.title: 'A tumour the size of a football saved my life'
articles.summary: Lisa Carroll, 47, who was diagnosed with rare form of ovarian cancer, urges women to check symptoms.
articles.body:
A mum-of-three who was diagnosed with a rare cancer has urged other women not to dismiss their symptoms.

When Lisa Carroll, 47, from Coventry, returned from a family holiday in August 2021, she thought she was suffering from irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), a kidney infection or something minor.

Instead, she was told it was mucinous ovarian cancer (MOC), one of the rarest forms of ovarian cancer in the UK.

"I thought I had possibly a bit of IBS or a kidney problem or something like that. I was in quite a lot of pain," she said.

After calling NHS 111, Carroll was sent to hospital in Coventry where medics discovered a 12cm cyst on her right ovary.

She was told it did not appear particularly sinister and was placed on a waiting list for surgery.

"Within a month, a cyst the size of a fist had grown to the point that I could feel it like a football in my stomach. Pain and discomfort got worse and I felt shattered emotionally and physically", she said.

By December, scans revealed the tumour had grown to 20cm and was beginning to rupture, so three days later she underwent an emergency procedure to remove the tumour, a fallopian tube, her appendix and surrounding tissue.

Two weeks later, doctors gave her the diagnosis.

The cancer is exceptionally rare, with only around 200 cases diagnosed annually in the UK, said Ovacome, an ovarian cancer charity.

"Some ovarian cancers are really sneaky, hang around for years and you've got no sign of any symptoms at all", said Carroll, who works as the CEO of Lifespace Trust, a Warwickshire-based charity for young people.

"The fact that mine grew so quickly was what alerted them as early as they did."

Yet despite losing her hair and enduring months of treatment, she says the biggest challenge was something she had not been prepared for.

"I got chucked into early menopause and that was the bit I massively struggled with. I didn't know what was depression and what was menopause."

"I didn't know what was a cancer symptom and what was a menopause symptom. I couldn't open the washing machine, the dishwasher or the oven. I couldn't cook anything on the hob because I'd just have this awful hot flush. I was forgetting words. I was incredibly emotional."

Today, Carroll is cancer-free and approaching the five-year milestone that will see her formally discharged from oncology care.

"I do not underestimate how fortunate I am that my long-term outlook is a lot brighter than for many," she said. "That brings with it a kind of survivor's guilt."

She has since became involved with Ovacome, which connected her with others facing the same fears.

"They became my safe space," she said. "They helped me to connect with other people who understood what I was going through. They made an incredibly scary and isolating time feel far more manageable."

Now preparing to take part in the charity's annual fundraising walk, Carroll hopes sharing her story will encourage others to trust their instincts and seek help when something feels wrong.

The fundraising walk takes place at Cannon Hill Park in Birmingham on Saturday.
